name: Hybrid Architecture
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Best of Both Worlds: Putting the Chain Where It Counts
lesson.summary: Real systems rarely put everything on-chain; hybrid architectures keep a small, tamper-evident anchor on the blockchain while doing the heavy lifting off-chain in ordinary databases, storage, or PKI.
lesson.body:
Alternative Technologies and Architecture Tradeoff already hinted at this chapter's conclusion: since blockchains are slow and expensive per byte stored, and traditional databases and PKI are fast, cheap, and flexible, engineers usually combine the two rather than picking one exclusively. The blockchain plays the role of an anchor of trust, a small, shared, append-only ledger that timestamps and tamper-proofs commitments about data that actually lives somewhere else.

The typical pattern works like this. Bulk data, documents, images, transaction details, personal records, is stored off-chain in a conventional database or file store. A cryptographic hash, a short, fixed-length fingerprint of that data, is written on-chain. Anyone who later obtains a copy of the off-chain data can hash it again and compare the result to the on-chain hash. If the two match, they know the data has not been altered since the hash was recorded, without the blockchain ever having had to store the sensitive data itself.

A concrete example: a supply chain traceability system. Each time a shipment changes hands, the company logs details such as weight, temperature readings, handler identity, and timestamp in an ordinary database it controls, then writes only the hash of that log entry to a shared ledger that all supply chain partners can read. Partners can later audit that no one silently edited a historical shipment record, since the hash would no longer match, while the bulk of sensitive commercial data stays in a normal, queryable, and deletable database rather than being permanently broadcast to competitors.

Traditional PKI vs DLT connects here too. Hybrid systems often use PKI-issued certificates to authenticate which organization submitted a given on-chain hash, combining the identity assurances of PKI with the tamper evidence of a shared ledger. Payment channels that settle only occasionally on-chain, oracle services that feed real-world data onto a chain, and off-chain storage networks paired with on-chain content hashes are all variations on this same hybrid idea.

For a skeptic, hybrid architecture is often the honest answer to whether something should be on a blockchain at all, because it keeps the one property a blockchain is genuinely good at, a shared timeline no single participant can quietly rewrite, without paying blockchain costs for everything else. It is also the architecture that makes later ideas in this chapter batch practically workable: when personal data needs to be deleted to satisfy a privacy law, you delete it off-chain, and the on-chain hash becomes meaningless without the data it once pointed to.
